sections.h: Jeremiah 50-51: the oracle against Babylon
sections.b: The longest oracle in Jeremiah is against Babylon, the empire Jeremiah had told Judah to serve (Jeremiah 27:6-8). Babylon is shamed in its gods Bel and Marduk, struck by a nation from the north, called 'Insolence', and repaid for the temple (Jeremiah 50:2, 28-32). It is the gold cup in the LORD's hand (Jeremiah 51:7), a mountain of ruin (Jeremiah 51:25) and a threshing floor ready for harvest (Jeremiah 51:33). Verses are used again from Jeremiah's own earlier poems (Jeremiah 6:22-24; Jeremiah 49:18-21; Jeremiah 10:12-16), and ciphers hide two names (Jeremiah 51:1, 41). The Greek Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew overall, and it lacks a block of verses here (Jeremiah 51:44b-49a).

sections.h: How Babylon fell, and how the oracle was read
sections.b: Cyrus took Babylon in October 539 BC, with little fighting (Nabonidus Chronicle; Cyrus Cylinder). Herodotus and Xenophon add that he diverted the Euphrates. The oracle's pictures of total ruin and emptiness did not happen at once, and readers differ: poetic exaggeration, fulfillment in stages as Babylon declined, or a still-future Babylon. Revelation takes up the cup, the call to leave and the stone thrown into water for 'Babylon the Great' (Revelation 14:8; 17:4; 18:4, 21).

common: Many readers take the poems of Jeremiah 50-51 as looking ahead to the fall of Babylon to Cyrus's Medes and Persians.
uncommon: Some futurist readers expect a rebuilt Babylon and a final destruction at the end of the age.

sections.h: Babylon, the last nation
sections.b: The Hebrew oracles against the nations in Jeremiah (chapters 46-51) end with Babylon, the nation that had been God's instrument against all the others. It is the longest oracle of the series. The order differs in the Greek, where Babylon comes after Egypt and the series stands in the middle of the book. The oracle treats Babylon as the other nations are treated: its gods are shamed, the LORD calls it to account, and a remnant of Israel is brought home. The collection lets Babylon's judgment settle all the earlier ones: the hammer that broke the nations is itself broken (Jeremiah 50:23; 51:20-24).

sections.h: Cyrus behind the Babylon oracle
sections.b: Cyrus is not named in Jeremiah 50-51 (he is named in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1). The 'kings of Media' roused against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11, 28) and the 'nation from the north' (Jeremiah 50:3, 41) match the army that took the city in 539 BC, when Median and Persian forces were joined under Cyrus. The call to leave Babylon (Jeremiah 51:45) belongs to the same years as Cyrus's edict that let the exiles go.

sections.h: The sea monster and the burned house
sections.b: In the Babylon oracle Nebuchadnezzar is both the last lion to gnaw Israel's bones (Jeremiah 50:17) and the sea monster who swallowed Zion and rinsed her out (Jeremiah 51:34). The final chapter retells his siege of Jerusalem, his judgment on Zedekiah at Riblah and the burning of the temple by his chief of the guard Nebuzaradan in his nineteenth year (Jeremiah 52:4-14). The three deportation counts in his seventh, eighteenth and twenty-third years are in Jeremiah 52:28-30.

sections.h: Leaving Babylon, and who was taken
sections.b: Jeremiah told the exiles to settle in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:5-7). The Babylon oracle tells them to leave when the city falls: 'Run from the heart of Babylon' (Jeremiah 50:8; 51:6, 45, 50). Israel and Judah come home together (Jeremiah 50:4-5, 19-20), and the LORD, their strong redeemer, argues their case (Jeremiah 50:33-34; 51:36). Jeremiah 52:28-30 counts those taken: 3,023, then 832, then 745, 4,600 in all, far fewer than the totals in 2 Kings 24:14, 16.
sections.refs: Jeremiah 50:4-8; Jeremiah 50:33-34; Jeremiah 51:6; Jeremiah 51:45; Jeremiah 52:28-30; 2 Kings 24:14

sections.h: Burned, plundered and avenged
sections.b: 'Vengeance for his temple' is the exiles' cry in the Babylon oracle (Jeremiah 50:28; 51:11, 51). Jeremiah 52:12-23 tells the end of Solomon's temple: Nebuzaradan burned the LORD's house, the Chaldeans smashed the bronze pillars, stands and Sea and carried the bronze to Babylon, and a long list of vessels was taken. The accounts of the pillars (eighteen cubits high, four fingers thick) and the pomegranates add detail not in 2 Kings 25. The Hebrew days of the fall differ: the seventh of Av (2 Kings 25:8) or the tenth (Jeremiah 52:12).

sections.h: The siege and fall, as Jeremiah tells it
sections.b: Jeremiah 52:4-14 dates the siege from the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year (January 588 BC) and the breach to the ninth day of the fourth month of the eleventh (July 586). The city was under siege for about thirty months, with the famine severe at the end. Zedekiah fled by night through the gate between the double walls toward the Arabah, was caught on the Jericho plains, and was taken to Riblah. Jeremiah's own experience of the siege is told in chapters 32, 34, 37 and 38.

sections.h: The river that Babylon stood on
sections.b: The Euphrates ran through Babylon. The Babylon oracle says its waters will dry up (Jeremiah 50:38; 51:36), that the fords are seized and the reed beds burned (Jeremiah 51:32), and also that the sea comes up over her (Jeremiah 51:42). The oracle ends with a scroll thrown into the middle of the Euphrates, to show that Babylon will sink and not rise (Jeremiah 51:63-64). Revelation 16:12 dries up the 'great river Euphrates' and Revelation 18:21 throws a millstone into the sea.

sections.h: Forgiven and not found
sections.b: In the Babylon oracle the remnant is those the LORD forgives: Israel's guilt 'will be looked for, but it will not be there' (Jeremiah 50:20). The return is of both houses together (Jeremiah 50:4), to the pastures of Carmel, Bashan, Ephraim and Gilead (Jeremiah 50:19).

sections.h: Bad shepherds and the lion's challenge
sections.b: Israel is a lost flock whose shepherds made them stray (Jeremiah 50:6) and whom the lions of Assyria and Babylon ate (Jeremiah 50:17). The LORD challenges every shepherd: 'Is there a shepherd who can face me?' (Jeremiah 50:44). The strong redeemer will bring Israel back to its own meadow (Jeremiah 50:19, 34).

sections.h: Bel, Marduk and the metalworker's idol
sections.b: The Babylon oracle opens with Bel and Marduk shamed (Jeremiah 50:2) and closes the idol theme with the hymn also in Jeremiah 10:12-16: every metalsmith is shamed by his idol, whose image is a lie with no breath in it, while the LORD made the earth (Jeremiah 51:15-19). The LORD will call Bel to account and take back what he swallowed (Jeremiah 51:44, 47, 52).

sections.h: 'As she has done, do to her'
sections.b: The Babylon oracle is the book's strongest statement of repayment in kind: 'Repay her by her own works; whatever she did, do it to her' (Jeremiah 50:29; compare 50:15; 51:24, 49). The LORD is 'a God of repayments' (Jeremiah 51:56). The speech of Zion, asking that her blood be on Babylon (Jeremiah 51:35), is answered by the LORD's promise to plead her case (Jeremiah 51:36). Readers differ on how such words should be prayed by Christians (see Romans 12:19).

sections.h: A covenant that will not be forgotten
sections.b: As Babylon falls, the people of Israel and Judah come weeping to Zion and 'join themselves to the LORD by a covenant for all time that will not be forgotten' (Jeremiah 50:5). The phrase echoes the everlasting covenant of Jeremiah 32:40 and links to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34, which Christians and Jews read differently.

sections.h: Babylon trampled flat
sections.b: 'Daughter Babylon is a threshing floor when it is being stamped flat. Just a little longer, and harvest time will come for her' (Jeremiah 51:33). The picture of judgment as harvest and threshing also appears in Isaiah 21:10 about Babylon and in Revelation 14:14-20.

sections.h: The ban on Babylon
sections.b: The nations called against Babylon are 'set apart as holy for war' (Jeremiah 51:27-28), and the LORD tells them to put Babylon 'under the ban' (Jeremiah 50:21, 26; 51:3). The language is that of Joshua's wars, turned on the empire that had destroyed the temple. In history Cyrus's army entered without wrecking the city.

sections.h: The King whose name is the LORD of Armies
sections.b: The Babylon oracle ends its poems with the LORD as 'the King' (Jeremiah 51:57), against the king of Babylon who thought himself master of the world. The book ends with a real king, Jehoiachin, released from prison and given a seat above the other captive kings (Jeremiah 52:31-34).

sections.h: How the book ends: Babylon, then Jerusalem, then Jehoiachin
sections.b: Jeremiah 50-51 turns the book's long judgment on Babylon, and ends with Seraiah's scroll sunk in the Euphrates and the note 'Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah' (Jeremiah 51:59-64). Chapter 52 is a retelling of 2 Kings 24:18-25:30 with additions: it shows the fall of Jerusalem and ends with the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon. The Greek Jeremiah is shorter in these chapters (no 51:44b-49a; no 52:2-3, 15, 27b-30).

sections.h: Zedekiah's end in Jeremiah 52
sections.b: Jeremiah 52:1-11 tells of Zedekiah's reign of eleven years, his revolt against Babylon, his flight from Jerusalem by night, his capture on the plains of Jericho, the killing of his sons and the officials of Judah at Riblah, and his blinding and imprisonment in Babylon until he died. Jeremiah had told him he would see the king of Babylon and go to Babylon (Jeremiah 32:4-5; 34:3), and promised that he would die in peace if he obeyed (Jeremiah 34:4-5).

sections.h: Released from prison
sections.b: Jeremiah ends with Jehoiachin: in the thirty-seventh year of his exile, in the year Evil-merodach began to reign, the king of Babylon lifted up his head, brought him out of prison, gave him a seat above the other kings, and a regular allowance for life (Jeremiah 52:31-34). Ration tablets from Babylon name him as 'Ya'ukin, king of Yahudu'.

sections.h: Jeremiah 52: the fall in detail
sections.b: Jeremiah 52 follows 2 Kings 25 closely, with a long list of the bronze and other vessels that were taken, the execution of the chief priest Seraiah and the deputy priest Zephaniah and others at Riblah, and three counts of exiles. Dates: the siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month (January 588 BC), the city was breached on the ninth of the fourth month (July 586), and the temple was burned on the tenth of the fifth month (Jeremiah 52:12).

sections.h: The Medes in Jeremiah 51
sections.b: The LORD rouses 'the spirit of the kings of Media' against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11) and calls the 'kings of Media, its governors and all its deputies' (Jeremiah 51:28). The Greek has the singular 'king of the Medes' in both. Isaiah 13:17 names the Medes too.
